intro:
Use it to name a field. It also carries what a reader needs to know about the field before filling it in: whether it must be filled, a hint such as a format or a limit, and an action at the far end of the line, such as a link to reset a password or a count of characters left.

Tie it to its control with `htmlFor`, or wrap it round the control. A label wrapped round a checkbox or switch reads that control's state: it fades when the control is disabled and turns to the destructive colour when the control is invalid. A label tied by `htmlFor` cannot see its control, so pass it `invalid` and `disabled` yourself.

`required` draws a mark for the eye only. Set `required` on the control too, because that is what a screen reader announces.

parts.Text: The field's name. A string passed straight to `Label` is wrapped in it for you. It truncates rather than pushing the action off the line, and the required mark is drawn after it.
parts.Hint: A quieter word or two after the name: a format, a limit, a unit. On an invalid label it turns to the destructive colour, so it can say what is wrong. Give it an `id` and point the control's `aria-describedby` at it, so a screen reader reads it too.
parts.Action: Pushed to the far end of the line, whatever its place in the markup: a link, a count, a small button, a switch.

examples.title: Actions on the line
examples.description: `Label.Action` sits at the end of the line: here a link to reset a password and a button that copies a key. A link inside it is drawn in the foreground colour and underlined on hover.

examples.title: Invalid and disabled
examples.description: A label tied by `htmlFor` takes `invalid` and `disabled`. When it is invalid, its hint turns to the destructive colour as well, so the hint can be the reason. Type a name that is not taken to clear it.

examples.title: Wrapped round a control
examples.description: Wrapped round a checkbox or a switch, the label reads the control: the disabled checkbox fades its label with nothing passed. Put a switch in `Label.Action` to set it at the end of the line.

notes:
### Required and optional

`required` draws an asterisk after the text. `optional` writes "Optional" after it instead, for a form where most fields are required and the few that are not need saying.

### Every attribute passes through

`Label` renders a `<label>` and passes everything to it, so `htmlFor`, `id` and the rest work as they do on the element.

### It renders on the server

`Label` has no client JavaScript. Its state reaches its parts through data attributes and CSS.
